General elections were held in Honduras on 30 November 2025. Voters elected the President, all 128 members of the National Congress, and 20 representatives to the Central American Parliament. Three major candidates are running for president: former Defense Minister Rixi Moncada for the Liberty and Refoundation Party, former Vice President Salvador Nasralla for the Liberal Party and former Tegucigalpa Mayor Nasry Asfura for the National Party. The election became heavily watched when U.S. President Donald Trump tried to influence the election in favor of Nasry Asfura after he publicly supported him. Trump has said that the United States would not give any financial aid to Honduras if Asfura does not win. Trump has also promised to pardon former President Juan Orlando Hernández, who was serving a 45-year prison sentence in the United States for drug trafficking. Hernández was released from prison on 2 December 2025. On 24 December 2025, Asfura was announced the winner of the presidential election. Asfura wrote on social media: "Honduras: I am ready to govern. I will not let you down."

An election for the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales was held between 1–30 August 2025. It was held at the same time as the party's deputy leadership election and other elections within the party. There were two candidacies for the leadership: a joint ticket of Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns running to be co-leaders, and Zack Polanski running to be solo leader. Polanski won the vote, gaining 84.1% of the votes.

The 2025 Philippine Senate election was the 35th election of members to the Senate of the Philippines for a six-year term. It was held on May 12, 2025, within the 2025 general elections. The following are serving a successive six-year term and are barred from seeking reelection. Nancy Binay (UNA), running for mayor of Makati On January 20, 2024, Binay stated in an interview on DWIZ-AM that she was "50 percent sure" that she would run for mayor of Makati upon the end of her term as senator. She confirmed her bid for the mayoralty on September 9. The incumbent mayor and Binay's sister Abigail is running for senator under the Nationalist People's Coalition. Koko Pimentel (Nacionalista), running for House representative from Marikina's 1st district Pimentel was rumored to run for representative from Marikina's 1st congressional district against Miro Quimbo. Pimentel did file to run on this district, but against incumbent mayor Marcelino Teodoro, husband of incumbent representative Marjorie Ann. Villar was then later seen as running for Congress. Villar then filed to run as representative, while her daughter Camille, the incumbent House representative is running for senator. Sonny Angara (LDP), appointed as Secretary of Education On July 2, 2024, President Bongbong Marcos appointed Angara, a term-limited senator, as secretary of education. On July 18, Angara resigned from the Senate a day before assuming office, leaving his seat vacant until his successor is elected in the regular election. Angara was previously term-limited. The 2025 New Jersey gubernatorial election took place on November 4, 2025, to elect the governor of New Jersey. Current Democratic governor Phil Murphy is term-limited and cannot run for another term. Democratic congresswoman Mikie Sherrill and Republican former state assemblyman Jack Ciattarelli ran to replace Murphy. The election had a high level of interest because many voters wanted change after two terms of the same party. Mikie Sherrill defeated Ciattarelli in the general election. She is projected to win Morris County, the first Democratic candidate for governor to do so since Brendan Byrne in 1973. She is set to become the second female governor in New Jersey history, following the election of Republican Christine Todd Whitman. She is also the first woman to win over 50% of the vote in the state's history, Sherrill was also strong enough to reverse the gains Ciattarelli had made in his much closer 2021 race, winning by a significantly larger margin statewide. Sherrill flipped back multiple counties that had supported Ciattarelli in 2021 or that President Trump had carried in 2024 (including Atlantic, Cumberland, Gloucester, Morris, and Passaic). By a much wider 13-14 point margin than Murphy’s 2021 win, indicating a swing back toward Democrats, as well flipping the state back to being more democratic. On 4 February 2025, a school shooting happened at, an adult education centre in Örebro, Sweden. Eleven people were killed, including the perpetrator, and six others injured. Reasons behind the attack are under investigation by the Swedish Police Authority and the Swedish Security Service. Six people were hospitalised. Swedish prime minister Ulf Kristersson said that it is the worst mass shooting in the country's history. The Swedish government and the Sweden Democrats unveiled plans to pass stricter regulations on firearms, including restricting access to semi-automatic weapons such as the AR-15.

General elections were held in Singapore on Saturday, 3 May 2025. All 97 members of the Parliament of Singapore, across 33 constituencies, were elected. Lee Hsien Loong did not lead the People's Action Party (PAP), as he had retired as prime minister and Lawrence Wong became Prime Minister after him on 15 May 2024. He became secretary-general of the PAP after Lee on 4 December 2024. The PAP has won the majority of seats in every election since independence. Under Article 65(4) of the Singaporean Constitution, a parliamentary term lasts a maximum of five years. However, the Prime Minister, with a vote from a majority of sitting Members of Parliament (MPs), can advise the President for early dissolution at any time. A general election must be held within three months of dissolution. The table below lists political parties elected or nominated in Parliament after the 2020 parliamentary election:

An early presidential election was held in South Korea on 3 June 2025. It was originally set for 3 March 2027, but the election was pushed forward after the impeachment and removal of Yoon Suk Yeol. The date of 3 June was due to the requirement by the country's constitution for an election to be held within 60 days of when the presidency becomes vacant. Since democratization and the creation of the Sixth Republic, this was the ninth presidential election, the second election after a presidential impeachment, and the first held in a different year than originally scheduled. Democratic Party nominee and former Opposition leader Lee Jae-myung defeated ruling People Power Party nominee Kim Moon-soo, and Reform Party nominee Lee Jun-seok in a landslide victory. Voter turnout was 79.38%, the highest since the 1997 presidential election. Democratic Party candidate Lee Jae-myung has had legal troubles that may ban him from being elected president. Under the Public Official Elections act, candidates who receive more than 1 million won in fines or any prison sentence are banned from serving as a public official for 5 and 10 years respectively. In March 23, Seoul High Court reversed a decision made sentencing Lee to one year in prison with a two-year probation, allowing him to run for public office again. However, in May 2, a speedy 10-2 judgement from the Supreme Court reversed the lower court's decision, and sent the case back to Seoul High Court for a retrial. The initial date of retrial was set at May 15, but was later delayed to June 18, which is after the election date. The two leading conservative candidates former Acting President Han Duck-soo and former Labor Minister Kim Moon-soo are expected to merge their campaigns, but made little progress in doing so. Kim has said that the PPP and its chair has moved to unify campaigns without talking with him. A party spokesperson said that it's likely the party would move to remove Moon-soo of his candidacy if he did not agree to unify with Duck-soo. The PPP confirmed early on May 10 that they would cancel the nomination of Kim, and instead nominate Han at an emergency convention the same day. Later that day, members of the PPP rejected a resolution making Han the party's candidate following an all-party vote, resulting in Kim's nomination being reinstated. Han later apologized for the candidacy dispute and withdrew from the election. The 21st Democratic Party presidential primary election was held on 27 April 2025. Lee Nak-yon hinted at a campaign for president at the National Convention for Constitutional Revision hosted by the New Future Democratic Party. On 30 April, Lee’s campaign advisor announced Lee’s candidacy registration, making his campaign official. However, on May 10, 2025, Lee decided against a run, and did not endorse a candidate. On 27 April 2025, the Rebuilding Korea Party announced their support for the Democratic Party's Lee Jae-myung for the presidency. On 19 April, the Progressive Party selected Kim Jae-yeon as its presidential candidate. However, she withdrew on May 9, 2025 saying that she wanted to stop the PPP, and endorsed Lee Jae-myung. The 2025 Nepal Teachers' Protest was a big strike and protest by school teachers across Nepal in April 2025. It was organized by the Nepal Teachers' Federation (NTF). The teachers were against a new School Education Bill from the government. They said the bill would reduce job safety, give too much control to the central government, and break earlier promises made to teachers' groups. After Nepal became a federal country in 2015, teacher hiring and management changed to local governments. Teachers' groups said this caused unfair rules and political problems. A new education law was proposed in 2023, but it was not passed for over a year and did not follow earlier agreements. On April 2, 2025, teachers from all 77 districts started an indefinite strike. Many gathered in Kathmandu, especially near Maitighar and New Baneshwor. Schools were closed and normal life was disturbed. The teachers wanted job safety, equal pay with civil servants, social security, and no handover of teacher management to local governments. - April 2: The protest started with a peaceful rally in Kathmandu. NTF asked the government to move the education bill to Parliament quickly. - April 14: Big rallies caused problems in traffic in Kathmandu. Maitighar Mandala and New Baneshwor were major protest sites. - April 21: Education Minister Bidya Bhattarai resigned because of the pressure from protests. - April 22: The National Examination Board delayed the Grade 12 exams that were to begin on April 24. - April 27: 27 teachers, one journalist, and police officers were hurt in a clash at Singha Durbar in Kathmandu. - April 30: The protest ended after a nine-point agreement was signed between the government and the NTF. It included job safety and a promise to pass the bill. The government invited teachers for talks, but early discussions did not succeed. Some human rights groups said the police used too much force. Talks on April 27 also failed to make an agreement. On April 30, after 29 days of protest, the strike ended with a nine-point agreement. It included job safety, respect for earlier promises, and faster law approval.

The 2025 New York City Democratic mayoral primary took place on June 24, 2025 to elect its Democratic candidate for the 2025 New York City mayoral election. Democratic socialist and Muslim follower Zohran Mamdani won the mayoral race, becoming the first Muslim and socialist candidate to win a New York City mayoral race since the 1990s. The main candidates of the NYC Democratic mayoral election included Mamdani, Andrew Cuomo, and Brad Lander. Mamdani received 44% votes in the first round and 56% in the second round. Cuomo received 36% votes in the first and 44% in the second. The turnout was nearly the same as in 2021.

The 2025 Norwegian parliamentary election took place on 8 September 2025. All 169 seats in the Storting were up for election. The current government of the Labour Party (Ap), led by Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, was re-elected. It has governed as a minority government since 2021, first in a coalition with the Centre Party until it withdrew from the government in 2025, and then as a single-party government. The list below contains the parties elected to the Storting in the 2021 parliamentary election and their current seat tallies. Exit polling forecasted that the Labour Party had won the election and that Jonas Gahr Støre would remain as Prime Minister. It showed that the Conservative Party had fallen to third place with the worst election result in 20 years while the Progress Party had overtaken them to be the second-largest party in the Storting. The red-green bloc was projected to win 87 seats, allowing Støre to continue as Prime Minister.

On October 1, 2025, the federal government of the United States began a shutdown at 12:01 a.m. EDT because congress was unable to pass a funding bill for the 2026 fiscal year. The shutdown happened because Democrats and Republicans did not agree over federal spending levels, foreign aid rescissions, and health insurance subsidies. The shutdown caused the furlough of roughly 900,000 federal employees and left another 2 million working without pay. While essential services such as Medicare, Medicaid, and the Transportation Security Administration continued, many agencies, including the National Institutes of Health, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the WIC program stopped working. The shutdown is the 11th government shutdown that resulted in federal employees being furloughed, the longest government shutdown in U.S. history, and the third shutdown during a Trump presidency, after the January 2018 shutdown and 2018–2019 shutdown. The shutdown ended on November 12, 2025.

The 2025 Tennessee's 7th congressional district special election were held on December 2, 2025, to fill the vacant seat in Tennessee's 7th congressional district. Republican Matt Van Epps won the election and will serve in the United States House of Representatives for the rest of the 119th United States Congress, which will end on January 3, 2027. The seat became vacant on July 20, 2025, after the resignation of Republican Mark Green. Green resigned after voting to help pass the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Primary elections took place on October 7, where Republican Matt Van Epps and Democrat Aftyn Behn won their primaries. In the December 2 general election, Van Epps beat Behn by 8.8%. More Democrats voted in this special race, more than they did during the 2024 elections. This is the strongest Democratic performance in this district during the 21st century.

On 21 November 2025, gunmen kidnapped 315 people from St Mary's School in Papiri, Niger State, Nigeria. No group has yet claimed responsibility for the attack. 303 students and 12 teachers were kidnapped. All other schools in Niger State, as well as many in nearby states, have closed as a result of the attack. Fifty students escaped on 23 November, according to the CAN, leaving 253 children in captivity. The attack caused fear in the area, and many families waited for news about their childern.

An election for the mayor of New York City was held on November 4, 2025. Democratic state assemblyman Zohran Mamdani won the election with 50.4% of the vote, beating Republican activist Curtis Sliwa and independent former Democratic governor Andrew Cuomo. This election had the highest turnout for a New York City mayoral election in decades, mainly because many young people registered to vote. Mamdani is set to replace Democratic incumbent Eric Adams on January 1, 2026. Mamdani will become the first Muslim and first South Asian mayor of New York City, as well as its youngest since 1892. Curtis Sliwa won the Republican Party primary since no one else ran.
The 2025 Romanian presidential election took place on 4 May (first round) and 18 May (second round) 2025. The winning candidate is Nicușor Dan with 53.60%.

The 2025 Western Australian state election was held on 8 March 2025 to elect the 42nd Parliament of Western Australia, including all 59 seats in the Legislative Assembly and all 37 seats in the Legislative Council.

The 2025 Virginia gubernatorial election was held on November 4, 2025, to elect the governor of Virginia. Glenn Youngkin could not run for re-election as the state's constitution doesn't allow it's governors to serve consecutive terms. Former Congresswoman Abigail Spanberger was elected governor, defeating incumbent lieutenant governor Winsome Earle-Sears. Spanberger is also the first woman to be elected Virginia governor. On 18 January 2025, Ali Razini and Mohammad Moghiseh, two senior Sharia judges, were shot to death at the Courthouse of Tehran which is where the Supreme Court of Iran is located in. The attack also injured another judge and a bodyguard. The perpetrator committed suicide soon after the shooting. In a message, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei offered his condolences for the “martyrdom” of both judges. President Masoud Pezeshkian said the "terrorist and cowardly" act must be followed up quickly by security forces and law enforcement.

Mass protests erupted in several cities in Iran at the end of December 2025. The protests continued into 2026. Human rights groups and news organizations reported that many people were killed or arrested during the government crackdown. The exact number of deaths is disputed. The protests were triggered by growing inflation, rising food prices, shortages linked to sanctions placed on Iran by other countries and also mismanagement of the government. The falling value of the Iranian rial also led to more protests. The protests first started in Tehran, the capital city of Iran, and then spread to other major cities across the country. Over time, the unrest went beyond dissatisfaction with the economy, with protesters calling for an end to the Islamic Republic and ruling of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Media reports described the protests as the biggest in Iran since the nationwide protests of 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini. The protest started on 28 December 2025 with shopkeepers and merchants ( known as the bazaaris) going on strike and closing their shops in Tehran's Grand Bazaar. The Bazaaris have played a central role in past revolutions. They are one of the 3 groups that define Iranian social life next to the Intelligentsia, the clerics. For centuries, these traditional marketplaces have functioned as more than just commercial hubs, also as political meeting places where different people from the community come together. The Grand Bazaar is more than 100 hectares big (147 football/soccer fields big) and 10 plus kilometers long and holds tens of thousands of shops selling everything from clothes, food, services and gold. It is a symbol of Tehran's old economy and dates back to the 17th century, during the Safavid period. On the 29th of December the head of the Central Bank of Iran, Mohammad Reza Farzin resigned as the protests spread to other cities. On the 30th December the protest spread to even more cities as well as several university campuses, leading students and other parts of the middle class to join. The end of the first phase was concluded with the widespread closures of almost 70% of the 31 Iranian provinces. In these first 4 days the level of violence from the government and its Islamic Revolutionary Guard against the protesters to stop them also got more significant. By firing live tear gas at protesters and arresting them. On January 1st the first official fatalities were reported. Dozens of arrests were made by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard, who were also firing live ammunition at protestors. This was later confirmed by several news sources because during phase 2 the internet was also shut down across the country. On the 2nd of January U.S. President Donald Trump reacted to violence happening during the protest, posting on his own social media platform, Truth Social. "If Iran shots [sic] and violently kills peaceful protesters, which is their custom, the United States of America will come to their rescue". On January 3rd the Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei states: "rioters must be put in their place" which led to more aggressive actions by the security forces on the protesters. Which leads to the security forces to begin more aggressive actions against protestors. The protest have now expanded to 25 out of the 31 provinces in Iran. On the 6th of January Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) a us-based organisation states that the death toll has now risen to 36. Which now leads the demonstrations into a new phase: On the 8-9th of January the death toll rises into the thousands. Making it one of the deadliest periods in the history of the current Iranian government. The exact number of deaths is very difficult to track because of the internet shutdown. The internet was shut down following a call by exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi for mass demonstrations at 8 p.m. on the 8th and 9th of January. People went to the streets and shouted: “Death to the Islamic Republic!” and “Death to the dictator!” or people called for the return of Pahlavi. Pahlavi also called on U.S. President Donald Trump and several European leaders to demand accountability from the regime. According to Amnesty International access to internet and telecommunications was cut in an effort to hide state violence. The blackout severely hampers the ability of victims, journalists, and rights groups to document abuses and gather evidence, while state-affiliated media and officials retain full internet access and continue spreading propaganda design to intimidate the public. Broad internet shutdowns of this kind serve a dual purpose: they conceal human rights abuses while simultaneously constituting violations in their own right, given that internet access is considered a fundamental right. This tactic is not new for Iran. During protests in November 2019, a near-total communications blackout was imposed while hundreds of protesters and bystanders were unlawfully killed over five days. A similar disruption occurred during the Woman, Life, Freedom movement in 2022. The current shutdown, however, is de longest the authorities have ever imposed. In the aftermath of the mass killings, thousands more protesters were arrested and a nighttime curfew was imposed in major cities, as heavily armed security forces patrolled the streets. According to multiple sources on the ground, residents were ordered not to leave their homes after 8:00PM, the Iranian Regime had imposed 'martial law'. Due to these measures the protest was briefly contained. Also in the aftermath footage began to emerge of a makeshift morgue at the Legal Medicine Organisation in Kahrizak, near Tehran. This was set up because the facility had gotten overwhelmed by the sheer amount of causalities. Amnesty International analysed five videos from the site and identified at least 205 distinct body bags. With further video showing a digital counter of the deceased reaching 250. BBC Persian published a report on instagram of the events on the 13th of January, quoting an eyewitness account in Kahrizak: “They [victims’ families] reached an autopsy hall where bodies were piled on top of each other… There was one room that was so full of bodies the door would not even open… Another room contained the women’s bodies.” On the 23rd of February 2026, the HRANA released The Crimson Winter. A comprehensive roughly 1,350-page document covering the first 50 days of the protests. From the 28 December 2025 to 15 February 2026. The report compiled through a coordinated, multi-team effort across HRANA. With team like Spreading Justice, the Pasdaran Documentation Project, and the Statistics Department. They drew on more than 143,330 reports from confidential and open sources. Beyond casualty figures, the report examined: patterns of violations including killings, injuries, arrests, coerced confessions, pressure on families attacks on medical neutrality. Forced confessions were characterised as a tool used systematically by authorities to control public narratives and intimidate the population. HRANA emphasised that the confirmed figures represent only the bare minimum and that the true scale of violence was likely considerably higher. The level of violence was difficult to examine because of the near-total internet blackout imposed by the regime which severely limited the flow of information. A second wave of protest began on the 21st of February, led by students (the Intelligentsia) at several universities. These demonstrations at universities continued to the 25th of February, with protesters chanting "Death to Khamenei" and displaying the Lion and Sun flag (a symbol of pre-revolutionary Iran). The 28th of February marks the start of the Israeli-United Stated strikes on Iran, leading to a full scale war in the region. Protesters used slogans about unity, freedom, economic problems and opposition to the government. Videos showed protesters chanting "Don't be afraid, we are together" and "Azadi" which means "freedom" in Farsi. Many slogans were directly against the government. Examples included "Death to Khamenei", "Death to the dictator" and "We don't want the Islamic Republic". These slogans showed anger at Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and rejection of the Islamic Republic. Some slogans referred to the Pahlavi monarchy, which ruled Iran before the 1979 Iranian Revolution. These included "Long live the Shah", "Reza Shah, may your soul be blessed" and "This is the final battle; Pahlavi will return". These slogans were used by some protesters, but they did not represent all protesters. Economic slogans were also used. Examples included "Death to inflation" and "Poverty, corruption, high prices - we'll go until overthrow". These slogans connected economic problems with anger against the government. Some protesters used the Lion and Sun flag. This symbol was used on Iran's national flag before the 1979 Islamic Revolution. After the revolution, the Islamic Republic replaced it with a new emblem. The Lion and Sun flag became a symbol of opposition to the current government. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty described it as a symbol of national pride, secularism and defiance of theocratic rule. The flag did not have only one meaning. Some people used it to show support for the former monarchy. Others used it more generally as a symbol of resistance to the current government. The symbol was also visible in protests outside Iran. In January 2026, a protester in London replaced the Iranian embassy's national flag with the pre-1979 Lion and Sun flag. In February 2026, protesters at a large rally also waved green, white and red flags with Lion and Sun emblems. Iranian officials reacted strongly to the protests. They said that people could speak about economic problems, but they also described parts of the protests as riots or unrest. Several officials connected the protests to public order, national security and foreign influence. Ali Khamenei, Supreme Leader of Iran, said officials should talk to protesters, but added that "rioters must be put in their place". Chief Justice Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i, the head of Iran's judiciary, said that the punishment for rioters would "be decisive, maximum and without any legal leniency". Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Speaker of the Islamic Consultative Assembly, said that some groups wanted to turn public demands into chaos. He also said that the security of the country had to be protected. Ahmad-Reza Radan, the chief commander of the Police Command of Iran, said: Important arrests were made of the main elements of the unrest, who will be punished after going through legal procedures. The protests also led to reactions outside Iran. Foreign governments, international organizations and human rights groups criticized the way Iranian authorities responded to the protests. Many international reactions focused on human rights, the right to peaceful protest and the use of force by security forces. U.S. President Donald Trump warned Iran not to use deadly force against peaceful protesters. The United States also criticized the treatment of protesters and people mourning those who had been killed. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International said that Iranian authorities used unlawful force against protesters. They called for an end to the violence and for the protection of people taking part in peaceful protests. The United Nations criticized Iran’s response to the protests. UN officials called on Iran to respect human rights, including the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression. Pope Leo XIV, the leader of the Catholic Church, said that he was thinking about people suffering in Iran and Syria. He called for dialogue and peace. The exact number of people killed, injured and arrested during the protests is disputed. Different sources give different numbers and the numbers changed as the crackdown continued. Internet restrictions made it difficult for journalists and human rights groups to check reports from inside Iran. On 13 January 2026, the Associated Press (AP) reported that HRANA (Human Rights Activists in Iran) had counted at least 2,000 people killed. AP said the number became clearer after people in Iran were able to make phone calls abroad again, after days of severe communication restrictions. On 27 January 2026, the AP reported that HRANA had counted at least 6,221 deaths. HRANA said the dead included 5,858 protesters, 214 government-linked forces, 100 children and 49 civilians who were not demonstrating. AP also reported that many more people were still feared dead. Human rights groups also reported mass arrests. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International said that Iranian security forces used unlawful force and firearms against protesters and made mass arbitrary arrests after the protests began on 28 December 2025. In February 2026, Human Rights Watch said that Iranian authorities carried out mass arbitrary detentions, torture and enforced disappearances after the crackdown. It said that the arrests were used to frighten the population after the protests. The protests did not have one clear leader. Many demonstrations were local or were organized through social media. However, several political and government figures were important because of their role in Iran's political system, the economy, the crackdown or international reactions. Ali Khamenei was the Supreme Leader of Iran during the protests. He was the highest political and religious authority in the Islamic Republic and was directly criticized during the protests. He was important because the protests were not only about the economy, but also about the political system that he led. He was killed in February 2026 during U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Masoud Pezeshkian is the President of Iran. His government faced pressure during the protests because of the economic crisis, the falling value of the rial and the spread of the protests. Mohammad Reza Farzin was the head of the Central Bank of Iran during the start of the protests. The Central Bank became important because the protests began after the Iranian rial fell to a record low against the United States dollar. Farzin resigned after the currency crisis became a major cause of public anger. Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i is the head of Iran's judiciary. The judiciary became important because many protesters were arrested and some later faced criminal charges. Ahmad-Reza Radan is the chief commander of the Police Command of Iran. The police were involved in the government response to the protests, including arrests and public order operations. Radan was important because the police played a direct role in the state response to the unrest. Donald Trump was the President of the United States during the protests. He was important to the international reaction because he warned Iran not to use deadly force against peaceful protesters. The 2025-2026 protests were part of a longer history of protest in Iran after the 1979 Iranian Revolution. Since 1979, several protest movements have challenged the Islamic Republic. These movements were not all the same, but many included anger about political power, limits on freedom, economic problems and the role of security forces. One important earlier protest movement was the 2009 Green Movement. It began after the disputed re-election of President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad. Many protesters believed that the election had been unfair. The protests became one of the largest challenges to the Islamic Republic since 1979. Later protests were often linked to economic problems as well as political anger. The 2019-2020 Iranian protests began after a rise in fuel prices. They quickly became wider protests against poor living conditions, corruption and the government. Iranian authorities responded with a violent crackdown and many people were killed or arrested. The 2022 protests after the death of Mahsa Amini were another major turning point. They were connected to women's rights, state violence and civil freedoms. The slogan "Woman, Life, Freedom" became one of the best-known slogans of that movement. The 2025-2026 protests brought together several older protest themes. Like the 2019-2020 protests, they began with anger about economic problems and living conditions. Like the 2022 protests, they also included wider criticism of the Islamic Republic and calls for political change.

An early general election was held in Japan on 8 February 2026 in all constituencies, including proportional blocks, to elect all 465 seats of the House of Representatives, the lower house of the National Diet. The election took place nearly four months into Sanae Takaichi's time as Prime Minister of Japan, which began on 21 October after she won the 2025 Liberal Democratic Party presidential election and formed the Liberal Democratic Party–Japan Innovation Party coalition (LDP–JIP). The main opposition was the newly formed Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA), a new political party formed as a merger between the primary opposition Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP) and Komeito, the LDP's former longtime coalition partner. The LDP won a historic landslide victory, with the party keeping its majority in the House and setting a new postwar record for the most seats won by a single party with 316 seats. This gave the party a two-thirds supermajority and passed the last record of 308 seats won by the Democratic Party of Japan in 2009 and the LDP record of 300 seats won in 1986. Meanwhile, the CRA lost more than two-thirds of its pre-election seats and leading to the resignations of party co-leaders Yoshihiko Noda and Tetsuo Saito after the election. Analysts said the LDP's victory was because of Takaichi's high personal popularity at the time of the election, mainly among young voters and conservatives.

On the night between 31 December 2025 and 1 January 2026, a fire broke out in a bar in Crans-Montana, Valais, Switzerland. There was a flashover. The alert to the police was given around 1.30am. Over 100 people were in the bar at that time, during end-of-year celebrations. According to first accounts, over 40 people were killed and at least 100 were injured. The Italian government speaks about more than 40 people killed, and at least 100 people injured. Media said that most of the injured people were gravely injured, with burns. Recently, the number of people affected were increased to over 40 dead, and at least 115, mostly gravely injured. People were taken to hospitals as far away as Lausanne, Geneva, Zürich and Stuttgart. Italy gave the rescuers access to a hospital in Milan that specializes in treating burns. During the night, more than 150 medical specialists helped the rescue efforts. A no-fly-zone was established over Crans-Montana. Many of the people were adolescents. On January 4, all 40 people who died have been formally identified. About half of them were minors, about half were Swiss. The cause of the fire is still unknown. At the moment, police think it was an accident. According to eye-witnesses, a bottle with sparklers was moved too close to the ceiling, which then caught fire. Swiss authoritties currently think this is the most likely scenario. A criminal investigation was started against the owners of the bar. Le Constellation was a bar, nightclub, and café in Crans-Montana, mainly popular with international tourists. It could hold 300 people and 40 could be accommodated on the terrace. The bar included a shisha and smoking area in addition to 14 TV screens for the viewing of sports, particularly football. The bar had been "a real institution", according to BBC News, and had "been around for at least 40 years". It was acquired and remodeled in 2015 by a married couple from Corsica who own several establishments in the region. Swiss media reported that guests previously rated the bar poorly on online rating platforms, complaining about poor treatment of personnel, a lack of professionalism, and security deficiencies. When it comes to fire protection, Switzerland has very high standards. Public places, such as bars, get checked regularly. It on the village or town to organise checks, for the bars and clubs there. Other restaurant owners said that the town did not do enough checks. Some restaurant-owners said they were checked twice in ten years. They spoke about Mafia-like structures that existed. The owner of the bar in question said there had been three checks in ten years, and that for everything, the correct procedure had been followed. An architect living told the New York Times that the emergency exists did not meet requirements, and that one had even been closed. The bar in question had not been checked for security since 2020. Swiss law mandates such checks every year or every second year. The youngest people among the dead and injured are 14 years old. They should not have been in the club past 10pm, without their parents. Also, it is currently unclear whether alcoholic drinks were served to them. In Switzerland, people below 16 are not allowed to drink alcohol.

The 2026 Hungarian parliamentary election is the tenth general parliamentary elections in Hungary since the change of regime on 12 April 2026. Péter Magyar's Tisza Party won a supermajority and Magyar was elected Prime Minister, ending Orbán's 16 year rule. According to Hungary's constitution, the election takes place in April or May of the fourth year following the election of the previous Parliament, and the President sets the specific date at least 72 days before the election. The day of the vote may not fall on a national holiday or public holiday (e.g. 1 May), nor on the day before or after, nor on Easter Sunday or Pentecost Sunday. Hungarian elections must be held on Sundays. on 13 January, 2026, President Tamás Sulyok called the elections for 12 April. The single-round election is regulated by Act CCIII of 2011. There are 199 members of the National Assembly, and the electoral system is a mixed majority system: 106 MPs are elected by a relative majority in individual constituencies, and 93 MPs are elected by proportional representation on party or nationality lists, with the addition of fractional votes. Since 2014, each of the Armenian, Bulgarian, Croatian, German, Greek, Polish, Romani, Romanian, Rusyn, Serbian, Slovak, Slovenian, and Ukrainian ethnic minorities can win one of the 93 party lists seats if they register as a specific list and reach a lowered quota of the total of party list votes. Fractional votes are those votes that did not win a mandate in the constituencies, and also include the winner's "surplus" votes that were not needed to win. Candidates who stood as independents, or were nominated by a party that did not have a national list, or did but did not reach the parliamentary threshold, cannot have their votes counted as a fraction of a vote. Thus, if such a candidate wins, the 'surplus' votes no longer needed to win are lost, while if he loses, all the votes cast for him are lost. To become a candidate for an individual constituency, 500 signatures must be collected under the electoral laws. One representative is elected in each individual constituency in a single-round, single-X vote, and the candidate who receives the most votes is elected. A party list can be nominated by a party that has an individual candidate in 71 constituencies, but at least in 14 counties and Budapest. To nominate a national list, the recommendations of 1% of the voters registered in the national register, but at least 1500 people, must be collected. Nationality voters may decide to vote for their nationality list, in which case they cannot vote for a party list. When the seats are distributed, votes from nationality lists are also taken into calculation. Hungarians outside the borders who do not have a Hungarian address may vote only on party lists. The list votes must be summed up. If a national minority secures all national list votes divided by 93, then divided by 4, they receive a preferential mandate. The number of preferential mandates obtained by national minorities must be subtracted from the total number of available list mandates. Parties that reach 5% (for dual lists, 10%, and for triple or more lists, 15%), National minorities that reach 5%. Fractional votes must be added to the parties' votes, while the preferential quota must be subtracted from the national minorities' votes. The mandates are distributed using the D'Hondt method: Create a table: the first row contains the votes, the second row contains half the votes, the third row contains one-third of the votes, the fourth row contains one-quarter of the votes, and so on. Each party/minority receives as many mandates as there are "circles" in their column. Nationalities that do not win a mandate can send one nationality representative to the National Assembly. The spokesperson has the same rights as MPs, except that he or she cannot vote on decisions of parliament. In the electoral system, the list is a closed list, and the order of the candidates on the list, as established by the parties, cannot be changed by the voters through preferential votes. Before the election, several well-known parties announced that they would not run in the election in order to ensure the victory of the most popular opposition party, Tisza. On 22 February 2026, Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera Cervantes, the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), and six others were killed in a security operation by the Mexican Army in Tapalpa, Jalisco, Mexico. The operation caused armed fights in the area, causing mass shootings, explosions and multiple vehicles and stores being set on fire throughout the state and much of the rest of the country. After El Mencho was killed, cartels began retaliatory attacks against the army and tourist spaces. The United States gave intelligence information to the Mexican government through a task force they created to fight against cartels. The clashes have caused many deaths for both the National Guard and cartel members, as well as at least one civilian death. An early indirect presidential election was held in Hungary on 11 August 2026 following the removal of Tamás Sulyok by a constitutional amendment. András Baka, former President of the Supreme Court nominated by the governing Tisza Party, was elected with a supermajority.

A referendum on the resumption of European Union membership negotiations was held in Iceland on 29 August 2026. Its result was to reject the proposal for continuing talks for the country to join the European Union. Iceland applied to join the EU in 2009, but negotiations have been suspended since 2013. The Yes campaign said that Iceland already follows many EU laws through the European Economic Area (EEA) but has no influence over EU decisions. Supporters also said it would be good for the economy. The No campaign focused on sovereignty, saying that EU membership could weaken Iceland's control over agriculture, fisheries, and natural resources. After the No campaign won, Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said she would respect the results and said that more talks of Iceland joining the EU would not start until after her term ended in 2028.

General elections were held in Zambia on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. In the presidential election, incumbent president Hakainde Hichilema of the United Party for National Development (UPND) was seeking a second term. His running mate was incumbent vice president Mutale Nalumango there were up aganist 13 other candidates, with the main challenge being from Brian Mundubile of the Tonse Alliance's National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), and his running mate Makebi Zulu. Hichilema won the election in the first round with 60.49% of the vote; Mundubile received 37.87%. In the National Assembly, the UPND won a majority, obtaining 160 of the 278 seats. The NRPUP came second, with 76 seats. Independents, smaller parties and directly appointed members received the remaining 42 seats. The 2026 election was the first election to use a new system for choosing members of the National Assembly. The new system was introduced by the Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025. Before the change, there were 156 elected seats in the National Assembly. The amendment added 70 more seats, bringing the number of constituency seats to 226. The ECZ announced the new constituencies on 16 April 2026. The amendment also added 40 more seats. These seats were set aside for 20 women, 15 youths and five persons with disabilities. The ECZ gives these seats to political parties based on the number of valid votes their presidential candidates received. These seats are not won by voting in individual constituencies. The 40 proportional-representation seats were allocated as follows: Persons with disabilities: 5 seats — UPND 3, NRPUP 2 Local council elections were held on 13 August 2026, at the same time as the presidential and National Assembly elections. Voters chose 116 mayors and council chairpersons and 1,858 ward councillors across all ten provinces. A total of 116 mayors and council chairpersons were elected. The results were: A total of 1,858 ward councillors were elected. The UPND won many wards in Southern, Western, North-Western and Central provinces. The NRPUP and other opposition candidates also won seats, especially in urban areas of the Copperbelt, Lusaka and Eastern provinces. Independent candidates also won many seats. In some councils, no single political party had enough councillors to control the council. This meant that parties and independent councillors had to work together to form a majority. The 2026 local elections were held under changes made by the *Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025*. One important issue during the campaign was the Constituency Development Fund (CDF). The CDF gives local authorities more work in areas such as community projects, local services and bursaries. Some of the main issues discussed during the campaign were: Urban areas: sanitation, rubbish collection, markets and drainage in cities such as Lusaka, Ndola and Kitwe. Rural areas: roads, clean water and the time taken to approve CDF projects. Party disputes: disagreements during party selections led some people to contest the elections as independent candidates. The local elections were managed by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ). Voting took place in all ten provinces. There were some delays in sending election materials to some rural wards, while counting was also stopped for a short time at some counting centres. After winning the election again, Hichilema thanked voters for their support in a Facebook post. He said his government would focus on national unity, peace and development. He also said his government would work on the concerns of people who voted for opposition candidates. On 15 August, a video was shared on social media in which Mundubile said that the UPND had hired people from Tanzania to interfere with the election. He said the UPND could not win the election and was trying to use what he called “Tanzanian tactics” to affect the result. Mundubile asked Tanzanians who were allegedly involved in election activities to leave Zambia. The Tanzanian government later denied sending anyone to Zambia to interfere in the election. It said that Tanzanian citizens in Zambia may have been taking part in the SADC election observer mission. Mundubile rejected the election result and said that he and his party would challenge the results through the courts. On 19 August, Citizens First presidential candidate Harry Kalaba called the elections one of the most deeply flawed in Zambia's history. He called for a full, open and independent review of the electoral process. Kalaba referred to reports of intimidation, interference with voting, problems with the handling of election materials and the uneven use of the law. He also praised the Tonse Alliance for what he called a “spirited and courageous fight” during the election. On 15 August, the European Union's Election Observation Mission released a preliminary statement about the election. It said that the election was competitive, but that restrictions on basic freedoms had made the election unfair for some candidates and parties. The mission also said that voting and counting at the polling stations it observed were generally open and clear, with party and candidate agents present. It raised concerns about the use of state resources during the campaign, restrictions on political parties and candidates, and the limited information given by the ECZ on election day. The EU mission stayed in Zambia to continue observing these developments. It said it would publish a final report with detailed recommendations within two months after the electoral process ended.

The 2026 SDF missile strikes in Hasakah refer to a series of attacks reported by the Syrian Ministry of Defence on 21 January 2026, during the first day of a declared ceasefire between the Syrian Armed Forces and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) in northeastern Syria. According to Syrian government statements, SDF units targeted army positions more than 35 times in Hasakah Governorate, resulting in the deaths of 11 soldiers and injuries to more than 25 others. The SDF denied responsibility for initiating the clashes and accused government forces of violating the truce. Ministry of Defense of Syria: Seven soldiers killed and 20 others wounded near a factory for manufacturing improvised explosive devices and drone munitions close to the al-Ya'rubiyah border crossing in the Hasakah countryside. The factory contained Iranian-made drones that the SDF was preparing to arm, and army units were working to secure it. The Syrian Army Operations Command: Four soldiers were killed in an attack by the SDF targeting army positions in Jabal Abdul Aziz in the Hasakah countryside and the village of Al-Sana'a, east of Aleppo. A four-day ceasefire between the Syrian government and the SDF was announced on 20 January 2026 in an effort to reduce tensions in northeastern Syria and reopen negotiations over security arrangements in Hasakah Governorate. The region has long been contested between Damascus and the Kurdish-led SDF, which is supported by the United States. Despite the agreement, both sides accused each other of preparing for further military action, raising concerns that the truce would be short-lived. According to the Syrian Ministry of Defence’s Media and Communications Department, SDF forces carried out more than 35 attacks on Syrian army positions on the first day of the ceasefire. The ministry stated that the assaults included missile fire, drone strikes, and small-arms attacks on checkpoints and military posts across Hasakah Governorate. Syrian state media reported that at least seven soldiers were killed in a drone strike near the al-Yaarubiyah border crossing, with additional casualties from follow-on clashes involving gunfire and armored The total death toll was reported as 11 soldiers, with more than 25 wounded. The SDF rejected the government’s account and said its forces were responding to violations by Syrian troops.

On February 10, 2026, a mass shooting occurred when she opened fire at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada. Of the people fatally shot, 6 were in the school, another died on the way to the hospital, and two others were killed at a house. 5 of the victims that died were children aged 12-13. 27 others were injured. The attack was the deadliest mass shooting in Canadian history since the 2020 Nova Scotia attacks. It was also the deadliest school shooting in Canada since the École Polytechnique massacre in 1989. In 2026, the school had about 175 students. At 1:20 p.m., Royal Canadian Mounted Police started to receive calls that an active shooting was taking place at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School. An emergency alert was sent out and students barricaded themselves inside the school. RCMP rushed to the school within two minutes and found the shooter had committed suicide at the school from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The suspect was first identified as "a female in a dress with brown hair". RCMP later confirmed 18-year-old Jesse van Rootselaar of Tumbler Ridge as the perpetrator. They stated that van Rootselaar was "born as a biological male" and had "identified as female, both socially and publicly" for around six years by then. The perpetrator was a trans woman. Van Rootselaar had a history of poor mental health. The shooter dropped out of school in 2022. Several World leaders expressed condolences to those affected by the shootings. The incident has re-sparked discussion about trans shooters. On May 7, 2026, it was announced by the provincial government that the school will be demolished and another school will be rebuilt to replace it.

The 2026 United States Senate election in Illinois will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the United States Senate to represent the State of Illinois. Current Democratic Senator Dick Durbin, who was re-elected in 2020 with 54.9% of the vote, decided not to run for a sixth term in office. This will be the first open Senate seat race in Illinois since 2010 and the first for this Class II seat since 1996, when Durbin was first elected. Primary elections were held on March 17, 2026. If elected, Juliana Stratton will become the second African American woman U.S. Senator elected from Illinois, after Carol Moseley Braun in 1999. On April 23, 2025, incumbent Senator Dick Durbin, who has held the seat since 1997, announced he would not run for re-election. The next day, Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton announced her campaign with the support of Governor JB Pritzker. Later, it was reported that U.S. Representatives Raja Krishnamoorthi, Robin Kelly, and Lauren Underwood were thinking about running. Kelly announced her candidacy on May 6, followed by Krishnamoorthi the next day, while Underwood announced that she would not run. On March 17, 2026, Stratton was announced as the winner of the Democratic primary, beating U.S. Representatives Krishnamoorthi and Kelly. The 2026 Scottish Parliament election will be held on 7 May 2026 to elect all 129 members of the Scottish Parliament. Going into the election, the Scottish National Party has the largest number of seats and currently leads a minority government with John Swinney as First Minister. The SNP has been in government since 2007 and is seeking a fifth term in office. The 2021 election saw the pro-independence parties (SNP and Greens) collectively achieving a majority of seats in the Scottish Parliament for the first time since devolution. In August 2021, the two parties entered into a cooperation agreement known as the Bute House agreement. In April 2024, Humza Yousaf ended the agreement, the Greens returned to the opposition and the SNP formed a new minority government. This triggered a crisis which ended with Yousaf's resignation and John Swinney becoming First Minister the following month. Scottish National Party – a centre-left party which promotes Scottish independence and social democracy, and supports rejoining the European Union. Scottish Conservatives – a centre-right to right-wing party which promotes conservatism, economic liberalism and British unionism. Scottish Labour – a centre-left party which promotes social democracy and British unionism. Scottish Greens – a left-wing party which promotes green politics, progressivism, republicanism and Scottish independence. Scottish Liberal Democrats – a centre to centre-left party which promotes liberalism, social liberalism and British unionism. It also supports rejoining the European Union. Reform UK – a right-wing party which promotes right-wing populism and Euroscepticism. Scotland is divided into 73 constituencies with roughly the same number of people in each one. Each of these constituencies elects one Member of the Scottish Parliament (MSP) using the First Past the Post voting system. These 73 constituencies are grouped into eight regions. Each of these regions elects seven MSPs using proportional representation which means that the total number of MSPs is 129. The election resulted in the Scottish National Party winning a fifth consecutive term in government. They won 58 seats, a net decrease of 6 from the 2021 election. However this was short of the 65 seats needed to form a majority government. The Scottish Greens won 15 seats (including 2 constituency seats), their best result to date at a Scottish Parliament election while Reform UK entered parliament for the first time with 17 seats. The Scottish Liberal Democrats also improved on its performance in 2021, winning 10 seats, a net increase of 6 from 2021. Scottish Labour had its worst-ever result with 17 seats, and the lowest share of the vote in both constituency and list votes for either Westminster or Holyrood since 1910. The Scottish Conservatives also saw its worst-ever result falling from second to fifth, and winning 12 seats. The election again resulted in the pro-independence parties again winning a majority of seats in the Scottish Parliament, repeating the results of the 2016 and 2021 elections. The SNP had won an outright majority in 2011.

The 2026 Los Angeles mayoral election will be held on November 3, 2026 to elect the mayor of Los Angeles, California. A nonpartisan top-two primary was held on June 2, 2026. Current mayor Karen Bass announced her re-election bid in July 2024. On June 8, 2026, Bass and city councilor Nithya Raman advanced to the general election in November. Most attention in the non-partisan primary was focused on Karen Bass, the current Democratic mayor; Spencer Pratt, a Republican reality television personality; and Nithya Raman, a Democratic city councilor. Pratt became popular with Republicans over his criticisms of Bass over her handling of the Palisades Fire, in which he had lost his home. Raman, a Democratic Socialists of America member, entered the race only hours before the filing deadline in order for the election to have a progressive candidate. The elimination of Pratt and other candidates set up a runoff election in which Raman is running against the incumbent Bass from the left. While both candidates are Democrats, Raman is also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, with the Los Angeles chapter supporting her on September 2, 2026.

The 2026 Labour Party leadership election was caused by Keir Starmer's resignation as Leader of the Labour Party and Prime Minister on 22 June 2026. Talks of a leadership election started after the party's poor results in the local elections, the Senedd election and Scottish Parliament election in May 2026, and grew after Andy Burnham's by-election victory in Makerfield. Starmer announced his resignation on 22 June and Burnham shortly announced his leadership campaign. Nominations from MPs opened on 9 July and closed on 16 July. Burnham received 379 nominations and was the only eligible candidate, as he was nominated by over 80% of all Labour MPs. At a final total of 94%, Burnham received the highest amount of MP nominations ever recorded in a modern Labour leadership contest. He became the Leader of the Labour Party on 17 July 2026, and is expected to become Prime Minister three days later, on 20 July 2026. 22 June – Sir Keir Starmer announces his resignation as Leader of the Labour Party 17 July – Result announced at Special Conference 20 July – Sir Keir Starmer resigns as Prime Minister. The winner is asked by King Charles III to form a new government. Burnham was the first to announce his candidacy for the leadership contest after Starmer's resignation announcement, saying that he "will put [himself] forward as part of this process." Wes Streeting, who was seen as a potential candidate, endorsed Burnham. Al Carns, who was seen as Burnham’s last possible opponent, decided not to run and endorsed Burnham. While not formally running in the race, Catherine West, the MP for Hornsey and Friern Barnet, was nominated by Neil Coyle after nominations had opened. This happened after it was mathematically impossible for a candidate other than Burnham to reach the needed level of 81 MPs. Catherine West did not launch a leadership bid and nominated Andy Burnham herself, she was nominated by one MP without her consent. On 7 August 2026, a 14-year-old student carried out a school shooting at the Debsirin School in Bang Kruai district, Nonthaburi province, Thailand. The shooting killed seven people and injuring around thirty others before committing suicide. The shooter also shot and killed his grandparents in Bang Bua Thong district before the shooting. The shootings were the nation's worst mass killing since the 2022 Nong Bua Lamphu massacre that killed 38 people.

The 2026 Zambian presidential election was held in Zambia on 13 August 2026 to elect the President of Zambia. It was held at the same time as the general election for the National Assembly and local government. Incumbent president Hakainde Hichilema of the United Party for National Development (UPND) won the election and was elected to a second term. His running mate was Vice-President Mutale Nalumango. Hichilema received 60% of the valid votes, while Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) received 38%. Hichilema received more than 50% of the valid votes, so there was no second round. The Electoral Commission of Zambia stopped counting for a short time on 14 August after reports of threats and attacks against election staff. Counting later resumed. The Electoral Commission declared Hichilema the winner on 18 August 2026. Mundubile rejected the result and said that he would challenge it in court. Hakainde Hichilema was the presidential candidate of the United Party for National Development (UPND). The party chose him as its candidate without opposition on 12 April 2026 at its party convention. Brian Mundubile was the presidential candidate of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP). The Tonse Alliance chose Mundubile as its presidential candidate in January 2026. Mundubile was first expected to contest the election under the FDD ticket. He later changed to the NRPUP ticket and filed his presidential nomination under that party in May 2026. The election initially had 14 candidates. They included Harry Kalaba of Citizens First, Fred M'membe of the Socialist Party, Given Katuta Mwelwa as an independent candidate, Kelvin Bwalya of Zambia Must Prosper, and Brian Mushimba of the Organised People's Party. Xavier Chungu of the Liberal Democratic Party later withdrew from the election while he was in detention. He could not campaign while in detention. The Electoral Commission of Zambia announced Chungu's withdrawal on 12 August, one day before the election. The ballot papers had already been printed. The ECZ said that votes for Chungu would not be counted as valid votes. The Electoral Commission of Zambia declared Hakainde Hichilema the winner of the presidential election on 18 August 2026. Hichilema was seeking a second term with Mutale Nalumango as his running mate. He defeated Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP). Hichilema won by 1,109,109 votes and received more than 50% of the valid votes. There was therefore no second round. Hichilema won the presidential vote in 124 of the 226 constituencies. Mundubile won in 102 constituencies. There were 8,786,300 registered voters. A total of 5,028,606 ballots were cast. This gave a turnout of 57.23%. Of the ballots cast, 4,902,050 were valid and 126,556 were rejected. The result gave Hichilema his second consecutive presidential victory. He had first won the presidency in 2021, when he defeated Edgar Lungu. Mundubile rejected the result and said that he and his party would challenge it in court. He alleged that there had been irregularities and electoral fraud. After the election, Hakainde Hichilema thanked voters in a Facebook post. He said his government would work for peace, unity and development. He also said it would listen to people who voted for other parties. On 15 August, Brian Mundubile accused the UPND of bringing people from Tanzania to interfere with the election. The Tanzanian government denied the claim. It said some Tanzanian citizens in Zambia may have been members of the SADC election observer team. Mundubile rejected the election result and said that he would challenge it in court. On 19 August, Citizens First leader Harry Kalaba called for an independent review of the election. He raised concerns about threats, voting problems, election materials and the use of the law. On 15 August, the European Union Election Observation Mission published its first report on the election. It said that many candidates took part in the election, but some rules made it harder for some candidates and political parties to compete equally. The EU observers said that voting and counting at the polling stations they observed were mostly open and clear. Representatives of political parties and candidates were also present. However, the observers raised concerns about the use of government resources during the campaign, some rules affecting political parties and candidates, and the amount of information provided by the Electoral Commission of Zambia on election day.

A general election will be held in Spain on 29 November 2026 to elect the members of the 16th Cortes Generales under the Spanish Constitution of 1978. All 350 seats in the Congress of Deputies will be up for election, as well as 209 of 267 seats in the Senate. After the 2023 election, Pedro Sánchez was able to get re-elected as prime minister of Spain and form a third government—made up of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and Sumar—with the support of Together for Catalonia (Junts). While Sánchez has thought about resigning twice, he is running for re-election. Because of the major housing protests in the autumn of 2026 and the parliamentary defeat to his housing relief plans by PP, Vox and Junts on 2 October, Sánchez called for a snap general election on 5 October.

The 2028 United States presidential election will be the 61st quadrennial presidential election. The election will be held on Tuesday, November 7, 2028, along with other state and federal elections. It will be the last presidential election to use population information from the 2020 census. Voters will elect a president and vice president to a four-year term. The winners of the election will be inaugurated on January 20, 2029. Donald Trump won the 2016 and 2024 elections and cannot run for re-election to a third term due to the Twenty-second Amendment. Trump's second term expires at noon on January 20, 2029. Donald Trump and JD Vance won the 2024 presidential election. Trump, who was elected president in 2016, but lost the election in 2020 to then-former vice president Joe Biden. Trump defeated incumbent vice president Kamala Harris, who began her campaign following Biden's drop out of the race. Republicans secured control of the Senate and retained a House majority. In the Electoral College, this results in major-party candidates primarily focusing their campaigns on swing states, which can swing between parties from election to election. The 2030 Romanian presidential election will be held in Romania in 2030. Voters will elect the President of Romania for a five-year term. The current president is Nicușor Dan. He was elected in 2025. In April 2026, he said that he would like to serve a second term as president. The President of Romania is elected by popular vote. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote in the first round, a second round is held between the top two candidates. Nicușor Dan is the current President of Romania. In April 2026, he said that he would like to run for a second term. He also said that his main focus was on his current term in office and that he would decide about the election later.

25 Churchill Place is a skyscraper in the eastern part of the London financial district Canary Wharf. Potential tenants included Aon, Deutsche Bank and News Corp. It is 118 metres (387 ft) and it opened in 2014, the same year when construction was completed after two years of construction.

The 25th Legislative Assembly of Ontario went from June 9, 1955 until May 4, 1959. It went until just before the 1959 general election. The majority party was the Ontario Progressive Conservative Party. The leader of this party was Leslie Frost. Alfred Wallace Downer was the speaker for the assembly.

The 2nd Punjab Regiment was a British Indian Army regiment from 1922 to the partition of India in 1947. The regiment was formed by the amalgamation of the following regiments: 1st Battalion, from the 67th Punjabis, formerly the 7th Regiment of Madras Native Infantry 10th (Training) Battalion, formed by redesignation of 2nd Bn, 67th Punjabis After the independence and partition of India in August 1947, this regiment became the Punjab Regiment (India).

The 39th G8 summit took place in Northern Ireland on 17th and 18th June 2013. The meeting was at the Lough Erne Golf Resort in Enniskillen, Northern Ireland In the Queen's speech at the state opening of Parliament in 2012, Elizabeth II said that "my government will use this opportunity to promote international security and prosperity." The gathering of the Group of Eight (G8) will be the 39th meeting in a series which began in 1976. Previous G8 summits have been hosted by the United Kingdom at London (1977, 1984, 1991) and Birmingham (1998) in England. The 2005 summit was in Scotland at Gleneagles. The G8 and the summit are part of a consultation process. The G8 is not an international organization. It is an informal group. The participants will be the "core members" of the group: A number of national leaders are traditionally invited to attend the summit. They are asked to participate in some, but not all, G8 summit activities. The summit meetings are intended as a way to resolve differences among the G8 members. Traditionally, the host country sets the agenda. As host, Prime Minister Cameron is expected to try to change the G8. He has criticised costs and questioned the value of G8 meetings. Discussions at the 39th G8 summit will include some issues which remain unresolved from previous summits. The G8 discussions will be about a range of topics, including Because of the nature of the summit, protest groups and other activists usually attend. The planning for the summit includes how to deal with these groups. Britain's leading aid groups and charities are planning a "propaganda offensive" which hopes to affect the food-dominated agenda for the G8.

The 3rd United States Infantry Regiment is a regiment of the United States Army. It currently has three active battalions. It's sometime called The Old Guard, as well as Escort to the President. The regimental motto is Noli Me Tangere (from Latin: – "Touch Me Not"). The regiment is a major unit of the Military District of Washington (MDW). The regiment is the oldest active duty regiment in the US Army. It was first created as the First American Regiment in 1784. It has been the official ceremonial unit of the US Army since 1948.
